sentences.text: They spent the whole afternoon at the rim of the biggest bowl.
Manuel had brought a folded picnic blanket and a small lunch of bread and cheese and hard-boiled eggs and oranges.
They ate slowly.
Manuel opened his sketchbook to a fresh page.
But he did not draw yet.
He talked.
"What you are looking at, mi hijo," he said, "is a laboratory.
It is a six-hundred-year-old agricultural laboratory built by the Incas.
Every terrace in that bowl is a different temperature.
The bottom of the bowl is about fifteen degrees warmer than the top edge.
That is more temperature difference than between here and the coast.
The Incas built the bowl so that they could grow the same crop at many different temperatures and see how each variety did.
They tested varieties of maize, of potato, of quinoa, of tomato, of coca, of a hundred other plants.
They kept the ones that grew well at each level.
Over generations, they bred varieties for the exact micro-climate of every valley in their empire.
This bowl was not for feeding people.
Not directly.
It was for figuring out what to plant everywhere else."
Diego looked at the bowl differently, then.
What had looked like an instrument became something more like a book — page after page of careful experiment, each ring a separate line of thinking.
He said, "How did they know?" Manuel said, "They watched.
For a very long time.
Hundreds of years, before this bowl was built, they were noticing how plants grew in different places.
This bowl was a way of putting all that watching into one place.
Instead of walking a whole day to see how maize grew at a slightly different altitude, they could walk down five steps."
Manuel picked up his pencil then, and began to draw — not the whole bowl, but one specific curve of one specific terrace, where a small stone drainage channel came out of the wall.
He drew with quick sure lines.
Diego watched.
Manuel's hand did not seem to think about what it was doing.
It just did it.

After maybe ten minutes he stopped, looked at what he had drawn, added one small dot with the pencil, and then wrote in the margin, in his small careful handwriting: Moray, July, still the same drainage as fifty years ago.
Small consolations.
Diego asked, "Have you been here before?" Manuel smiled.
"Twenty-eight times, in my life.
First when I was twenty-one and a young architecture student.
This sketchbook has drawings of Moray from every decade of my life.
I always come back.
It teaches me something new every time.
Or I am ready to see something new.
Either way."
The next morning they drove to Maras.
The salt pans were less than half an hour from Moray, cascading down a steep white and gold hillside above a small stream.
There were, Manuel said, about six thousand small rectangular salt pools built into the hillside — each maybe three meters across, each shallow and terraced above and below its neighbors.
The whole hillside looked, from above, like an enormous mosaic of pale gold and white tiles.
Manuel led Diego down the narrow paths that ran between the pools.
In several of them, women in bright pollera skirts were working — raking crystallized salt out of the drying pools into small baskets.
Manuel greeted a few by name.
They knew him.
He had been coming, he told Diego, since long before Diego was born.
They sat on a low stone wall above the pools with their lunch.
Manuel opened his sketchbook.
But before he drew, he said, "This place, Diego, is even more interesting than Moray, in a way.
The Incas did not build the salt spring.
The spring was here already — a natural underground source of very salty warm water, coming out of the mountain.
What the Incas did was design the whole system that turns that water into salt.
Every pool feeds the pool below it.
The water flows by gravity from the spring at the top, along channels the Incas cut, and enters each pool at exactly the right rate.
When a pool has enough water, its owner closes a small stone gate at the entrance.
The sun and wind evaporate the water, over about three weeks, until only the salt is left.
The salt is scraped out.
The pool is opened again.
The next batch comes in.
This has been done — the same way, by the same families — for five hundred years.
Every pool belongs to a specific family in the villages down below.
It is passed from parent to child."
Diego said, "So it is not owned by one person." Manuel said, "No.
Every family has ten or fifteen pools somewhere in the mosaic.
Together, the whole hillside is worked.
If your neighbor's pool leaks, you help fix it, because if it leaks it might damage yours.
Everyone works together to keep the channels running.
Nobody is in charge.
The system runs itself.
It has run itself for centuries.
That is what I want you to see.
That the Incas did not just build things.
They designed how people would live with each other around the thing they built.
That is much harder than building."
That afternoon, Diego did something he had not planned to do.
He took out the small plain notebook he had brought with him for school — he had thought he might do homework in the evenings — and he opened it, and he tried to draw one of the salt pools.
It was harder than he had thought.
His lines were not sure.
The pool did not look like a pool; it looked like a wobbly rectangle.
He crossed it out.
He tried again.
He crossed that out too.
Manuel, beside him, did not comment.
He did not offer help.
He worked in his own sketchbook.
After a few tries, Diego stopped crossing out.
He let the wobbly rectangle stay.
He added the small stone gate at the entrance.
He added the water.
He wrote in the margin, in his round eleven-year-old handwriting: Maras pool, July.
Try again next year.
When he looked up, Manuel was smiling slightly.
Manuel said, "That is exactly right.
That is what the whole sketchbook is.
Try again next year." And he did not say more.
